title: A Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 1)
shortDescription: The PCM has detected a fault in the variable valve timing (VVT) system on the intake camshaft of Bank 1.
fullDescription: This DTC indicates the powertrain control module has identified an abnormal condition with the intake camshaft VVT actuator on Bank 1. The VVT system uses oil pressure controlled by an electronic solenoid to advance or retard the camshaft phaser, which adjusts valve timing for optimal performance, fuel economy and emissions. A failure can result from low or contaminated engine oil, a stuck phaser, faulty solenoid, electrical issues, or a stretched timing chain that misaligns the camshaft to crankshaft.
safetyImpact: Engine may run rough, lack power, or stall. Long-term operation can damage the timing chain, phaser, or catalytic converter.

causes.cause: Low or dirty engine oil restricting VVT solenoid flow
Faulty intake VVT solenoid (oil control valve)
Stuck or damaged intake camshaft phaser on Bank 1
Damaged wiring or connector to the VVT solenoid
Stretched timing chain causing camshaft-crankshaft misalignment

symptoms: Rattling or ticking noise from the valve cover area at startup

fixSteps.title: Check Engine Oil
fixSteps.instruction: Verify oil level and condition. Top up or change oil with the manufacturer-specified viscosity. Old or low oil is the most common root cause for VVT codes.

fixSteps.title: Scan and Record Freeze Frame
fixSteps.instruction: Use an OBD-II scanner to record freeze frame data. Note RPM, coolant temp and load when the fault set; this helps isolate solenoid vs phaser issues.

fixSteps.title: Test the Intake VVT Solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the intake oil control valve on Bank 1. Disconnect, measure resistance with a multimeter and compare to spec (typically 6.9-7.9 ohms). Replace if out of spec.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check the VVT solenoid harness for chafing, oil contamination, and verify good ground. Backprobe the connector while running to confirm PCM commands the duty cycle.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Camshaft Phaser and Timing Chain
fixSteps.instruction: If solenoid tests good, remove the valve cover and inspect the phaser for play, the timing chain for stretch (compare timing marks), and tensioner for wear. Phaser replacement often requires special tools.

faq.q: Is it safe to drive with a VVT code?
faq.a: Short trips at moderate speed are usually OK, but extended driving with a VVT fault can damage the phaser, timing chain, or catalytic converter. Repair as soon as practical.

faq.q: Will an oil change fix a VVT code?
faq.a: If the cause was old or wrong-viscosity oil, a fresh oil and filter change with the correct grade often clears the symptom. If the code returns within a few drive cycles, the solenoid or phaser likely needs replacement.

faq.q: How much does a VVT solenoid cost?
faq.a: OEM VVT solenoids run $40-$120 each plus 30-90 minutes of labor. A camshaft phaser replacement is far more expensive — typically $600-$1,500 — because timing components must be removed.

fullDescription: This DTC indicates the powertrain control module has identified an abnormal condition with the intake camshaft VVT actuator on Bank 2. The VVT system uses oil pressure controlled by an electronic solenoid to advance or retard the camshaft phaser, which adjusts valve timing for optimal performance, fuel economy and emissions. A failure can result from low or contaminated engine oil, a stuck phaser, faulty solenoid, electrical issues, or a stretched timing chain that misaligns the camshaft to crankshaft.
safetyImpact: Engine may run rough, lack power, or stall. Long-term operation can damage the timing chain, phaser, or catalytic converter.

causes.cause: Low or dirty engine oil restricting VVT solenoid flow
Faulty intake VVT solenoid (oil control valve)
Stuck or damaged intake camshaft phaser on Bank 2
Damaged wiring or connector to the VVT solenoid
Stretched timing chain causing camshaft-crankshaft misalignment

symptoms: Rattling or ticking noise from the valve cover area at startup

fixSteps.title: Check Engine Oil
fixSteps.instruction: Verify oil level and condition. Top up or change oil with the manufacturer-specified viscosity. Old or low oil is the most common root cause for VVT codes.

fixSteps.title: Scan and Record Freeze Frame
fixSteps.instruction: Use an OBD-II scanner to record freeze frame data. Note RPM, coolant temp and load when the fault set; this helps isolate solenoid vs phaser issues.

fixSteps.title: Test the Intake VVT Solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the intake oil control valve on Bank 2. Disconnect, measure resistance with a multimeter and compare to spec (typically 6.9-7.9 ohms). Replace if out of spec.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check the VVT solenoid harness for chafing, oil contamination, and verify good ground. Backprobe the connector while running to confirm PCM commands the duty cycle.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Camshaft Phaser and Timing Chain
fixSteps.instruction: If solenoid tests good, remove the valve cover and inspect the phaser for play, the timing chain for stretch (compare timing marks), and tensioner for wear. Phaser replacement often requires special tools.

faq.q: Is it safe to drive with a VVT code?
faq.a: Short trips at moderate speed are usually OK, but extended driving with a VVT fault can damage the phaser, timing chain, or catalytic converter. Repair as soon as practical.

faq.q: Will an oil change fix a VVT code?
faq.a: If the cause was old or wrong-viscosity oil, a fresh oil and filter change with the correct grade often clears the symptom. If the code returns within a few drive cycles, the solenoid or phaser likely needs replacement.

faq.q: How much does a VVT solenoid cost?
faq.a: OEM VVT solenoids run $40-$120 each plus 30-90 minutes of labor. A camshaft phaser replacement is far more expensive — typically $600-$1,500 — because timing components must be removed.

The VVT system uses oil pressure controlled by an electronic solenoid to advance or retard the camshaft phaser, which adjusts valve timing for optimal performance, fuel economy and emissions. A failure can result from low or contaminated engine oil, a stuck phaser, faulty solenoid, electrical issues, or a stretched timing chain that misaligns the camshaft to crankshaft.
safetyImpact: Engine may run rough, lack power, or stall. Long-term operation can damage the timing chain, phaser, or catalytic converter.

causes.cause: Low or dirty engine oil restricting VVT solenoid flow
Faulty intake VVT solenoid (oil control valve)
Stuck or damaged intake camshaft phaser on Bank 1
Damaged wiring or connector to the VVT solenoid
Stretched timing chain causing camshaft-crankshaft misalignment

symptoms: Rattling or ticking noise from the valve cover area at startup

fixSteps.title: Check Engine Oil
fixSteps.instruction: Verify oil level and condition. Top up or change oil with the manufacturer-specified viscosity. Old or low oil is the most common root cause for VVT codes.

fixSteps.title: Scan and Record Freeze Frame
fixSteps.instruction: Use an OBD-II scanner to record freeze frame data. Note RPM, coolant temp and load when the fault set; this helps isolate solenoid vs phaser issues.

fixSteps.title: Test the Intake VVT Solenoid
fixSteps.instruction: Locate the intake oil control valve on Bank 1. Disconnect, measure resistance with a multimeter and compare to spec (typically 6.9-7.9 ohms). Replace if out of spec.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Wiring
fixSteps.instruction: Check the VVT solenoid harness for chafing, oil contamination, and verify good ground. Backprobe the connector while running to confirm PCM commands the duty cycle.

fixSteps.title: Inspect Camshaft Phaser and Timing Chain
fixSteps.instruction: If solenoid tests good, remove the valve cover and inspect the phaser for play, the timing chain for stretch (compare timing marks), and tensioner for wear. Phaser replacement often requires special tools.

faq.q: Is it safe to drive with a VVT code?
faq.a: Short trips at moderate speed are usually OK, but extended driving with a VVT fault can damage the phaser, timing chain, or catalytic converter. Repair as soon as practical.

faq.q: Will an oil change fix a VVT code?
faq.a: If the cause was old or wrong-viscosity oil, a fresh oil and filter change with the correct grade often clears the symptom. If the code returns within a few drive cycles, the solenoid or phaser likely needs replacement.

faq.q: How much does a VVT solenoid cost?
faq.a: OEM VVT solenoids run $40-$120 each plus 30-90 minutes of labor. A camshaft phaser replacement is far more expensive — typically $600-$1,500 — because timing components must be removed.
